title: The rcCRO Episode 1: The Reactive Manager Problem
summary: Episode 1 of the rcCRO: Paula Hansen (DocuSign), Stevie Case (Vanta), and Josh Kanagy (Hightouch) on manager coaching, spans of control, AI, and hiring.
body_markdown:
There are CROs, and then there are really cool CROs.


**The rcCRO** is Hyperbound's new monthly series where we bring really cool CROs together to talk through the sales leadership problems they're dealing with right now.


Episode 1 is The Reactive Manager Problem. Hyperbound co-founder Atul Raghunathan sits down with Paula Hansen (CRO, DocuSign), Stevie Case (ex-CRO, Vanta), and Josh Kanagy (CRO, Hightouch) to talk about why so many frontline managers spend their week rescuing deals while rep behavior stays the same.


[Go here to watch the full episode](https://hyperbound.ai/on-demand/rccro-s1e1-reactive-manager-problem)


Below is each question Atul asked and how each CRO answered, lightly edited for length and clarity.


‍


## Managers rate their coaching highly. Reps don't. What closes the gap?


**Atul:** You've all been in the first-line manager seat. 93% of managers rate their own coaching quality as high. Only 62% of reps agree. What explains that gap, and what closes it?


**Paula Hansen, DocuSign:** The first-line manager job is the toughest job in the company. You're getting requests from management above to execute, and you're dealing with a group of individuals who all have their own remits, personalities, and day-to-day challenges. The key starts with realizing that coaching is incredibly valuable and that people actually crave it. Many first-time managers don't realize that's part of their job. Beyond the mindset, it's about giving first-line managers the tools, the capabilities, the expectations, and the freed-up capacity to provide that coaching.


**Stevie Case, Vanta:** There's a real disconnect around what coaching is. In a hypergrowth company, half or more of your managers are probably in a management role for the first time. A lot of first-time managers think coaching is structured feedback on specific opportunities or next steps in a deal. When ICs think about coaching, they're thinking, "How can I improve myself and change the way I operate so I get promoted?" That's the kind of coaching frontline managers don't know how to do, are a little intimidated by, and struggle to find time for.


I'm a big fan of the saying that you should expect what you inspect. What we typically inspect in a sales org is the outcome: pipeline, stage progression, all the metrics AI can now inspect. It's rare that we inspect the coaching itself and its quality. There's a lack of frameworks, so a lot of frontline managers are improvising.


**Atul:** There are two parts to coaching. There's the procedural side, which is tracked by all the metrics we look at. And there's the human side: how are you developing me as a person and preparing me for the next step? The manager has the remit to do both and the training to do neither.


**Josh Kanagy, Hightouch:** Two words Stevie used need to be separated for frontline managers: coach and inspect. They often get conflated into one act and called coaching. Inspection is a distinct activity. Deal inspection, thinking about how to progress a deal, becomes a stand-in for coaching. Coaching is skill development. That's a lot different from offering sage advice on how to handle a prickly buyer. Part of closing the gap is helping frontline leaders see the difference and making sure there's a place for each.


**Paula Hansen, DocuSign:** Look at a professional athlete. Think about the time they put into skill development: time with their coach, getting feedback, reviewing tape, understanding the skills they need to bring to the game, versus just looking at how they're playing in the game. If we only talk about the deal, we miss the areas of development that get you ready before you get to the deal. That's the opportunity we have now as CROs.


‍


## What would you take off a manager's plate?


**Atul:** If you could take one thing off a manager's plate with extra resources, like an assistant or tooling, what would it be, and what would make them a better coach?


**Stevie Case, Vanta:** There are so many things pulling at them. What's ridiculous is that now that AI tooling is taking some things off their plate, there's a huge movement to increase manager span. Everyone is talking about managers taking 12 people, 20 people, why not 30? That ignores the hard part of coaching, the human part. You still have human beings on these teams who need coaching that can't be automated.


The number one thing I'd take off their plates is internal noise: the internal meetings and other work that doesn't generate value or build their skills. And we still need to keep managers at a reasonable span. We're feeding them a lot of data now, and they have the harder job of interpreting it. While they focus on that, giving them a framework for exactly what we want them to coach matters more than ever. In a lot of sales orgs, coaching gets left up to vibes.


**Atul:** What spans are you working with, and how does that play into this?


**Josh Kanagy, Hightouch:** At Hightouch, we try to operate at 6 to 1 in enterprise, and we're a little more comfortable at 8 to 1 in mid-market. We're constantly fighting that as we grow. It's very difficult to hire great frontline sales leaders, and the plan doesn't go away because hiring is slow. So hiring has to be a focus as an input into all of this.


But I'm with Stevie. We have to resist the urge to change spans of control. A large part of a frontline leader's job is understanding where each individual is today, their skill and their will, and building specific plans with them. There's a cost to increasing spans of control, even in a much more information-rich world, and that's a trap teams can fall into.


**Paula Hansen, DocuSign:** I agree 100%. Our spans are similar: closer to eight AEs per manager in enterprise and closer to ten in commercial. I think we've already hit what I'd consider the optimum.


The part we're not talking about enough is that AI is also part of what we're all selling. Customers expect your organization to help them put it into practice and get an ROI. That takes a whole other level of conversations and skills from account executives, which may require more coaching, not less. So we can't just double the span of control and keep everything else the same. Everything about customer engagement and customer expectations is changing, and you have to make room for that kind of development.


‍


## Are the new manager tools actually helping?


**Atul:** Even with all these tools emerging, win rates and conversion are getting harder. Are the tools that help managers just one more thing to check, or are they adding a meaningful advantage?


**Stevie Case, Vanta:** We're seeing some advantage, but it's been an evolution. At the beginning there was an experimentation phase: arm everybody with whatever they're interested in and let them find the value. There was a tremendous amount of noise, and some signal came through. I think it's reasonable to expect a 20% to 30% increase in productivity in any given part of the business, and we've seen about that across most of our functions.


We did a time study with our sales and SDR teams. The goal was to take 10 hours a week of busywork off quota-carrying reps, and we succeeded. Then more things filled their time, and the question became whether those things are actually valuable. The bar is higher now. If a buyer gets on the phone with a human, they expect real expertise, much more than a year ago when that person was there to facilitate a transaction. So we're getting more productivity, but there's more the team has to achieve, and it adds to the list of things managers need to coach.


**Atul:** Paula, that ties into what you said earlier about AEs needing more skills than two or three years ago. What are the top skills you've seen change?


**Paula Hansen, DocuSign:** One is applying your technology in your customer's environment. Customers expect you to understand their use case at a specific level, including their environment and integrations, and to articulate the measurable outcomes of their investment. Years ago you could throw together an ROI based on loose assumptions and move an investment forward. Now customers want to know upfront what the business impact will be, how they'll measure it, and over what time frame. That's why you see roles like FDEs emerging, focused on applying the technology and the impact it drives.


The good news is AI can help with that relevance. It pulls a lot of information from inside your organization and outside it. But that can be a lot of volume and noise. Finding the signal and the context, and helping people apply it in a specific way, is where the opportunity still lies.


**Josh Kanagy, Hightouch:** The buyer is evolving, and the asymmetry of information that used to exist is gone. A customer is often far down the decision-making path before they ever engage a vendor. That's a different skill for an AE than educating through outbound motions that lead to developing a champion. An extremely informed customer wants to start the conversation with very specific questions about how our solution will play out in their business. These are subtle shifts, and they require coaching that's timely and aware of how those dynamics are changing.


‍


## Is 15 minutes of coaching per rep per week enough?


**Atul:** The sales process has gotten more complicated and more technical, and the buyer is more informed. The pressure is on AEs and, as a result, on frontline managers. The average frontline manager today has about 15 minutes of dedicated coaching time per rep, per week. Is that enough? What's the ideal number, and what should a frontline manager be doing to coach?


**Stevie Case, Vanta:** Fifteen minutes is clearly not enough. It's wild that's all it is for what most leaders see as the highest-value thing frontline managers do. In a way, AI has helped with inspection, but it's also created an explosion of data. Parsing out what matters has become very hard, and what should drive productivity is creating a lot of slop in many organizations.


My role as CRO has become much more about getting down to the clear signal and not feeding my frontline managers every data point they could imagine. Twelve to 18 months ago, at the start of the AI wave, we went through the phase of "Here's thousands of data points. Figure it out." We've pulled far back from that. Now managers get a very short list of data points and one priority a week: "This week it's discovery. Here's what we're inspecting for, here's the framework, and here's what we want you coaching around." That simplicity matters more than ever as you scale.


**Atul:** Are there signals you'd call out as particularly good, as opposed to the noisy ones?


**Stevie Case, Vanta:** The problem is that the signal that matters changes all the time. That's changed the kind of people we need in RevOps. We've moved from a team of administrators who build tools and pass data along to very smart people who have a real point of view.


It's also changed how I run forecasts. A year ago our cadence was traditional: everybody in the room, talk about the deals, talk about the key metrics. Now we spend less time forecasting because I can gather a lot more signal asynchronously through AI and automated analysis. When we get together, I bring far fewer data points, usually the top two or three red flags that week. Some weeks that's a conversion metric at a specific funnel stage. Some weeks it's the attach rate for a specific product. We pick those signals week to week, and it helps the team focus on what matters today.


**Josh Kanagy, Hightouch:** Back to the 15 minutes: clarity on the expectations of the operating cadence is really important. As we onboard new leaders, making sure their calendar is aligned to what's required to be successful can't be overlooked. Managers can get comfortable and stop believing coaching needs to happen the same way. Time has to be carved out for it every week. It's no different from pipeline generation. If it's a key input into your business, the time has to be there. So the first thing leaders need is clarity on what the operating cadence looks like over a day, a week, and a month.


I also love what you said about simplicity, Stevie. Simplifying complex things has to be a top two or three item on any leader's list. We got into a world with such a proliferation of data that, with good intentions, we tried to show everyone how much insight we could give them. It had a paralyzing effect. So we've gone back to "This is the dashboard, these are the inputs I need you to focus on." If we take care of those, the extraneous data points take care of themselves. Scoreboard watching isn't a coaching motion. That's the postgame press conference.


**Paula Hansen, DocuSign:** Focusing on outputs has been a big part of running businesses for a long time, and it's still important, but AI can show you outputs pretty clearly. The question is which behaviors, inputs, and activities you want people to drive. Frontline managers used to go searching for everything. There was a dashboard for everything, and the number of dashboards, clicks, and filters it took to get to the information was significant. We've moved from what I call a pull motion to a push motion: we push recommendations to frontline managers and ICs about where to focus today and tomorrow. Simplifying what's in that push is really important so it's not overwhelming.


That has created more time for curiosity, role-playing, scenario planning, and the real work of deciding how to grow the business, grow the account, and help the customer succeed. AI plays a role there too, because it's a safe space to role-play, admit you don't know something, and ask questions you feel you should already know the answer to. The manager still plays a big part: being in the role-play and asking what we learned and how we'll apply it differently. Given what customers expect now, the number of scenarios is exponential. You have to think through all of them and the decision paths you want your people to take, which will require more coaching, not less.


‍


## How do you know a manager is overwhelmed?


**Atul:** Enablement exists, but it's ultimately the manager's job to make sure reps are prepared for every one of those scenarios. I love the idea of moving from a pull motion, where the manager consumes data, to a push motion, where the manager receives the relevant signals. Still, we see a lot of managers biting off more than they can chew, and that's likely leadership's responsibility. How do you know a manager is overwhelmed? Is it forecasts slipping, win rates, something else?


**Stevie Case, Vanta:** So much of what matters with managers now is human. It may sound old-school, but it's sentiment, retention, and attrition. The market is wild right now. There are exciting opportunities everywhere, and employees will stay because they feel a place is making them better, giving them better future prospects, and developing them. Attrition is the number one indicator of whether your managers are coaching and developing the team. You could have a team getting no coaching that still hits the number because of great product-market fit, and they could be miserable.


That's what makes the frontline manager role so challenging now. It's not just the mechanics of how you sell. It's personal and human. You need a better handle on human psychology and on what greatness looks like, and that's asking a lot of a first-time manager. The job is much harder now, and when it's done well, it's very hard to pin down and measure.


**Paula Hansen, DocuSign:** The more technology we have, the more emphasis it puts on human skills. We talk a lot about what the top rep does and how to replicate that across the organization. You may want the same outcome and the same process, but how each person gets there will be unique to who they are. One of the biggest mistakes new managers make is assuming all their sellers should operate the way they did as a seller.


You want consistency, frameworks, and process, but you need to understand who each person is, what motivates them, where they get satisfaction in their work, and where they're strong or weak in the process. Then you need to have a comfortable conversation about where they need development and make clear you're part of that growth. That puts more responsibility on the frontline manager, which is already a hard job. But it's an exciting one, because people are fascinating, and for the right person who wants to lead, it's really fulfilling.


**Josh Kanagy, Hightouch:** I want all our managers to understand that coaching and developing their people is a competitive advantage. We have to recruit with that promise and deliver on it to get people to stay. Employee retention begins and ends with development. A-players want to be developed. If they're not getting coached, they'll find an employer that will coach them, plain and simple.


At the same time, individual contributors need to understand that the expectation is to seek coaching and to participate in their own rescue when they don't understand something. It's not just about the metrics. It's about how we work together to make hitting the metrics we all care about easier. Those agreements need to be in place as people join the company.


**Paula Hansen, DocuSign:** One signal for me is the percentage of hiring a manager does from inside versus outside. You always want a balance. Internal hires show career development and progression, and outside hires bring new perspectives and experiences. If a manager's internal promotion percentage gets really high, that tells me they're overwhelmed. They're looking for the easy hire, someone who maybe doesn't need coaching because they've already been successful at the company. If you aren't willing to bring in people from the outside, it signals you don't want to do the heavy lifting: the coaching, the onboarding, and setting someone up to succeed.


‍


## Is coaching reflected in manager comp plans?


**Atul:** We all agree internal development is very important. Is it reflected in managers' comp plans in any meaningful way?


**Stevie Case, Vanta:** We haven't experimented with comp yet, but I think there's real merit in it. We're at a moment where we need to question how we measure manager success. In our last company survey, I got feedback along the lines of, "I'm being asked to do this set of things, but my performance review is tied to whether I hit the revenue target." So it's the right moment to ask those questions.


What has shifted before comp is the makeup of the team. We've made larger investments in L&D, enablement, and our people team than I've seen before, and that reflects a growing desire for development. One of the biggest shifts is a desire to see what great looks like from other people. We're doing less measurement of what great sounds like day to day and more "Let's play the tape, learn from your peers, and hear what greatness sounds like." I think comp changes will come.


**Josh Kanagy, Hightouch:** We haven't either. We're very differently resourced than my friends here.


**Paula Hansen, DocuSign:** We haven't tied it to compensation either. It's a tricky decision because outcomes matter. We're a publicly traded business, and we have to post results every 90 days. That said, there are a lot of supplemental ways to reinforce the behaviors you want. We do a lot with SPIFFs. We have one right now called Customer First, which recognizes someone who made a decision that was right for the customer, even if it wasn't good for us in the near term. That's taking the long view. People nominate each other and say, "You need to hear this story."


Reward and recognition, what you highlight at all-hands, and what you showcase as great to the rest of the company all matter. The key with compensation, like everything else we've talked about, is simplicity. Put too many dials into it and you lose the ability to drive the outcomes you're looking for.


**Stevie Case, Vanta:** The thing that's missing today is that we compensate frontline managers on the outcome. Underneath that, a lot of them don't yet believe coaching changes the outcome, or the time horizon is so long that they don't feel they have the luxury to do it. They're focused on this quota, this period. As leaders, we have to persuade frontline managers that coaching pays off and prove that it will move results, even if not today or tomorrow. That lack of belief is something we'll all have to address.


**Josh Kanagy, Hightouch:** When we hire external leaders, there's a strong desire for them to prove they belong. That's a natural feeling. A new leader doesn't have the market or product knowledge to help much in early-stage work, so they gravitate to late-stage deals. You don't need to know a ton about the business to help manage a procurement discussion or a commercial offer. Like a moth to the light, new leaders get drawn to the back end of sales cycles because they can show impact almost immediately. Then they get stuck there.


I'm constantly telling them they'll make the biggest difference by focusing on stage zero through stage three. If they invest that time in understanding what great looks like there and coaching that behavior, the outcomes take care of themselves. So I want to relieve new hires of the belief that they need to rescue us at the end of a deal. We have plenty of people who can help close. We hired you, you belong here, and we believe in you. Now go work way upstream with the team, and your impact will be bigger and faster. That's a permission you have to give new people.


**Paula Hansen, DocuSign:** It's almost like changing the title from manager to player-coach. You're part of the iteration, the learning, the growth, synthesizing data into context, and driving strategy. If the expectation is that you know all of that yourself and then teach your ICs, it's daunting, and it will never make the top of the list compared with managing opportunities in the 11th hour.


I also think managers should have a lot more customer-facing time over time. Nothing turns people into player-coaches more than being in front of customers. We're all there together, asserting a point of view, then reflecting on how it went and what we'd do differently. The market is moving so fast that the message that landed with customers a month ago could be very different from the one landing now. You have to learn that in real time and build an environment that keeps iterating.


**Josh Kanagy, Hightouch:** I'm a huge believer that the answers and the truth lie outside the four walls of our office. Go out and find it, learn it, and experience it.


‍


## How should the manager's day-to-day change?


**Atul:** Josh, to your point, the vast majority of coaching still happens at stage four and beyond. And Paula, to yours, the manager's ideal workflow is becoming more customer-facing, with the manager as the one who gathers and applies insights. Any hot takes on how the manager's day-to-day job should change in this era?


**Stevie Case, Vanta:** Managers need far more expertise, and that's true for ICs too. Managers used to be able to skate by without knowing the product in depth or having industry expertise. That's not true anymore. Buyers come to the conversation better educated and with a point of view. Your AE has to answer deep questions and deliver real value, and if you show up as a manager and can't add value on top of that, your team starts asking why you're there. They can get coaching from AI and data from lots of places.


Managers will have to up their game. There's a level of professionalism, polish, and expertise that will be expected, unlike what we've seen before. My hope is that it makes the frontline manager role more prestigious. Too many people see it as a stepping stone they have to get through to climb into leadership. But it's the highest-leverage role on the team, because they're in the trenches with ICs helping get it done. The bar is going to get a lot higher, and so is the opportunity for impact.


‍


## Have you changed how you hire managers?


**Atul:** The personality the role requires is changing too. Have you changed your hiring practices to account for that, or is it still early?


**Josh Kanagy, Hightouch:** We haven't changed practices, but we keep iterating on the profile we're looking for, and some process change comes with that. I'm not hiring as many frontline leaders as Paula and Stevie, but we're hiring a lot of them, and we're applying what's working to what we need to keep growing.


Going back to the professional athlete: the game tape exists, and there's a huge amount of data and insight. So how do we make sure managers focus on performing better in the under-pressure moments, the customer-facing interactions and meetings where the rubber meets the road? There's also a lot of coaching needed in what I call the gray area, the selling that happens between the stages and the EQ it requires. I want my frontline leaders focused there.


One thing we haven't talked about is the second-line leader. I need second-line leaders creating the conditions for frontline leaders to flourish and thinking programmatically across the business, while frontline leaders do the deal-specific and rep-specific work. Keeping those lines clear helps both.


**Paula Hansen, DocuSign:** There's a saying: plan your work and work your plan. The ratio between those two has to shift because of expectations. Years ago it was 20% planning your work and 80% working your plan. Now it's almost flipped, or needs to flip, to 80% thoughtful planning and 20% running it. Planning covers so much: who you hire, how you onboard them, how you frame the opportunity, where you focus, and which inputs you coach to, measure, and build programs around.


From a hiring perspective, self-awareness and curiosity are two skills I've always valued, and they're becoming even more important. Self-awareness means acknowledging there's always an opportunity to get better. Curiosity means being curious about your business, about the insights being served to you, and about the difference between IC A and IC B and how to get the best from both. Customer-facing time is a big part of that, and not just at the tail end of a deal.


**Stevie Case, Vanta:** Curiosity and grit are the one big change in how we hire managers now. A couple of years ago, we'd go to market, sell candidates on the opportunity, tell them everything great about the company, and get them excited to join. It sounds counterintuitive, but we've almost completely reversed that. We approach manager recruiting with an anti-sell.


We're looking for people with intense curiosity and grit who can navigate the amount and rate of change. So there's an explicit part of our recruiting process where we tell managers we're excited about: this will be extremely hard. Here are the things that make the job hard, here's what you'll struggle with, and here's what's not going well on your team. We want people who will fight through that and don't expect a perfectly set table where they crank a couple of dials and get a great outcome. There are candidates we once would have courted that we now actively exit from the process, because they don't have the determination to navigate the rate of change.


**Josh Kanagy, Hightouch:** The curiosity piece comes through in hiring. Candidates with real curiosity see through the anti-sell to the opportunity. It's on full display when you're deep in the anti-sell conversation and they say, "No, I understand what's at stake, and I'm still excited about the opportunity despite the tough days ahead."


**Paula Hansen, DocuSign:** You have to be inspired by the chaos and the increasing rate of change, and see it as a personal development opportunity. For the right person, that's incredibly rewarding. But they have to be willing to put in the effort, deal with ambiguity, and iterate. The idea that you lock something and it's done is naive. That's where self-awareness matters: How's it going? Did we get it wrong? Do we need to iterate? It's very likely you won't make all the right decisions or recommendations, and you'll have to learn and iterate from there.


‍


## Closing thoughts


**Atul:** As the role gets more ambiguous and needs more iteration and strategy to get right, we're putting more pressure on frontline managers. I love the idea of an anti-sell in hiring: let people know what they're getting into. Anything you want to close on?


**Paula Hansen, DocuSign:** It's an exciting time. The pace of technology innovation, the pace of change, and everything AI makes possible will change everything for everyone. We need to embrace that, move past debating it, and move into applying it. That's the leadership opportunity for all of us.


**Josh Kanagy, Hightouch:** While the impact of AI is new, history is full of major periods of uncertainty and transformation for leaders. The cause may be novel, but it isn't new ground. It's about finding leaders who get out of bed every day excited to make their people better. If that's the motive they bring to all the chaos and ambiguity, I feel pretty good about our odds. That drive is what will separate the best managers from the rest of the pack.


**Stevie Case, Vanta:** There's a real moment of opportunity for anyone in tech, and especially in go-to-market, to question what the job is now. The boundaries are flexible. If you're a builder, if you have grit, if you're creative, you can have impact far beyond the classic scope of the role. The top 10% or 20% of people in go-to-market who embrace this moment will transcend what it means to be a seller, and they'll become the next wave of founders, builders, and creators. In go-to-market, we're close to the customer and understand how customers think about value. If we think differently about how to harness that, what's possible gets much bigger.
